article.title: Why Feature Importance Does Not Tell You What Will Happen If You Change the Feature
article.why: Separate predictive explanations from causal claims before designing interventions.

paragraphs.en:
Feature importance tools help us understand how a predictive model uses information. SHAP values, permutation importance, coefficients, and related methods can reveal which variables strongly influence predictions. But an important predictive feature is not automatically a lever that a business can change to improve the outcome. Prediction and causation answer different questions.

Imagine a model predicting insurance purchase. Recent hospital visits may receive high SHAP importance. The model has learned that customers with more visits tend to have different purchase probabilities. It would be absurd, however, to conclude that the company should cause customers to visit hospitals more often in order to increase insurance purchases. The variable is informative because it reflects underlying circumstances, not because manipulating it would necessarily create the predicted effect.

The distinction becomes less obvious with actionable-looking features. Suppose app usage is strongly associated with higher spending. A team might propose a campaign to increase app usage and expect spending to rise. But high-value customers may already be more engaged and therefore use the app more. An unobserved factor such as loyalty could cause both behaviors. Increasing app usage alone may not reproduce the spending difference seen in observational data.

SHAP explains a model’s prediction relative to a reference distribution. It can answer questions such as why Customer A received a higher score than Customer B or which features contributed most across a dataset. It does not, by itself, estimate the outcome that would occur under an intervention that changes one feature while holding the causal system together.

This matters because business recommendations often move from description to action. ‘Customers with Feature X have higher predicted conversion’ is a predictive statement. ‘Changing Feature X will increase conversion’ is a causal statement. The second requires stronger assumptions or evidence. Randomized experiments are often the clearest approach when the feature corresponds to a controllable treatment. Quasi-experimental designs, causal graphs, instrumental variables, matching, or doubly robust estimators may help when randomization is not feasible.

Data leakage can make the problem worse. A feature measured after the outcome process has already started may be extremely predictive but useless for intervention. For example, a customer-service event triggered by an imminent purchase could appear highly important even though it is a consequence or near-consequence of purchase intent.

Feature importance can still be very valuable. It helps diagnose models, identify suspicious dependencies, understand segment differences, and generate hypotheses. It can also reveal variables worth investigating causally. The key is to label the conclusion correctly.

A practical review can classify important features into several groups: controllable treatments, customer states, proxies, contextual variables, and possible leakage. For controllable features, ask whether experimental evidence supports intervention. For state variables, use them primarily for segmentation or prediction unless a causal pathway is established.

Teams should also distinguish individual explanations from population conclusions. A positive SHAP value for one customer does not mean the feature has a positive average causal effect across all customers. Interactions and correlations can make local explanations especially difficult to generalize.

The safe workflow is therefore: use feature importance to understand the predictive model; form hypotheses about mechanisms; identify what can actually be changed; and test causal effects before converting those hypotheses into policy. A model can tell you what information helps predict an outcome. It cannot automatically tell you what action will create that outcome.
paragraphs.zh:
SHAP、permutation importance與coefficients可以解釋模型如何使用資訊，但predictive importance不等於causal effect。醫院就診次數可能高度預測保險購買，卻不代表讓顧客多去醫院就會提高購買。App usage與高消費相關，也可能只是loyalty同時造成兩者。

SHAP回答的是feature如何影響prediction，而不是介入改變feature後outcome會怎樣。從「Feature X的人conversion較高」跳到「改變Feature X會提高conversion」需要randomized experiment或其他causal methods支持。重要features可分成controllable treatment、customer state、proxy、context與possible leakage，再決定是否適合施策。Feature importance適合診斷與產生hypothesis，但不能自動轉成policy。
paragraphs.ja:
SHAP、permutation importance、係数はmodelが情報をどうpredictionに使うかを説明しますが、predictive importanceはcausal effectではありません。病院受診回数が保険購入を強く予測しても、受診を増やせば購入が増えるとは言えません。App usageと高利用額の関連も、loyaltyが両方を生んでいる可能性があります。

SHAPはfeatureがpredictionへどう寄与したかを示し、featureを介入で変えた場合のoutcomeを直接推定しません。「Feature Xの顧客はconversionが高い」から「Feature Xを変えればconversionが上がる」へ進むにはrandomized experimentやcausal methodが必要です。重要featureをcontrollable treatment、state、proxy、context、leakage候補に分類すると施策判断が安全になります。

vocabulary.usage: An important feature is not always a lever.
Manipulating a feature may not create the effect.
Instrumental variables can support causal identification.
A feature may be a proxy for loyalty.

business.term: SHAP tells us what drives the prediction, not what will happen if we intervene on that variable.
business.explanation: 避免把模型解釋直接當成施策因果。

sources: SHAP model explanation; causal inference; randomized and quasi-experimental design.
